title: A Comparison of Machine Learning Methods for the Prediction of Traffic Speed in Urban Places

authors.name: Josep Maria Salanova Grau
authors.affiliation: Centre for Research and Technology Hellas

authors.name: Georgia Aifadopoulou
authors.affiliation: Centre for Research and Technology Hellas

abstract: Rising interest in the field of Intelligent Transportation Systems combined with the increased availability of collected data allows the study of different methods for prevention of traffic congestion in cities. A common need in all of these methods is the use of traffic predictions for supporting planning and operation of the traffic lights and traffic management schemes. This paper focuses on comparing the forecasting effectiveness of three machine learning models, namely Random Forests, Support Vector Regression, and Multilayer Perceptron—in addition to Multiple Linear Regression—using probe data collected from the road network of Thessaloniki, Greece. The comparison was conducted with multiple tests clustered in three types of scenarios. The first scenario tests the algorithms on specific randomly selected dates on different randomly selected roads. The second scenario tests the algorithms on randomly selected roads over eight consecutive 15 min intervals; the third scenario tests the algorithms on random roads for the duration of a whole day. The experimental results show that while the Support Vector Regression model performs best at stable conditions with minor variations, the Multilayer Perceptron model adapts better to circumstances with greater variations, in addition to having the most near-zero errors.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2019 article has seen clear scholarly uptake, with 83 citations in OpenAlex and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of its cohort. Its influence is concentrated in traffic prediction, traffic control, and transportation optimization research, indicating that the comparison of machine learning methods has been useful as a reference point for subsequent work on urban mobility forecasting.

Full narrative

Published in Sustainability by a team from Aristotle University of Thessaloniki and the Centre for Research and Technology Hellas, the article compares machine learning approaches for predicting traffic speed in urban settings. The citation record shows that the paper quickly entered the research conversation and has maintained steady attention over time, with citations appearing consistently across 2020–2025 and continuing into 2026.

The downstream literature suggests that the paper’s main value lies in method selection and benchmarking for traffic forecasting. Most citing works are themselves articles or conference papers, and the dominant concepts among those citations center on traffic prediction and management, traffic control, transportation planning, and time-series forecasting. That pattern indicates the paper has been used less as a general theory contribution and more as a practical methodological guide for researchers building or evaluating predictive systems for urban transport.

The venue profile reinforces that reading: the work is cited within sustainability, sensor, computer science, and applied transport journals and proceedings, including repeated reuse in venues such as Sustainability and Communications in Computer and Information Science. The citing landscape also spans a broad international base, with particularly visible activity from China, India, and the United States, and a strong concentration in education-sector institutions.

Beyond citations, the record also shows 83 documented downstream reuses, matching the citation total in the available reuse graph. Scite reports 32 citation instances, 31 of them mentioning the work, which is consistent with the article being actively referenced in later discussions of machine learning for traffic prediction. Public-discourse and event-data signals are quiet in the available record, so the clearest evidence of impact remains scholarly uptake rather than broader public attention.
